newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S. faces uphill fight on labour at WTO.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. faces uphill fight on labour at WTO.

text.p: The United States faces an uphill battle on labour issues at next week's meeting of World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministers, but hopes to win a global agreement to eliminate duties on information technologies.

A successful Information Technology Agreement (ITA) at the WTO meeting in Singapore would energise the process of opening markets and help President Bill Clinton assert his leadership on trade after putting the issue on hold during the presidential election campaign, trade analysts said.

It could also underscore the benefits of global trade deals at a time when the Clinton administration is preparing to battle Congress over trade negotiating authority to add Chile to the North American Free Trade Agreement.

"I think it is very important that the American people have confidence that a body like the WTO can deliver ... on expanding market access opportunities," Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters. Negotiators in Geneva have been trying to finalise details of the proposed ITA pact -- which would remove tariffs on computers, software and telecommunications equipment by 2000 -- in time for next week's WTO meeting.
Singapore will host the first ministerial meeting of the WTO, successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, from December 9-13.

Barshefsky said at a news conference on Wednesday that a statement last week by Asia-Pacific leaders showing support for the global accord set the stage "for what should be doable" at the WTO meeting.

"The ITA should be able to be concluded at Singapore," Barshefsky said. But she said more work was needed by negotiators on product coverage and the staging of tariff reductions. Barshefsky also expressed concern about the stance of the European Union in the ITA negotiations.

"More progress will have to be made attitudinally, particularly with regard to the EU," Barshefsky said. "We have still a very schizophrenic Europe and that won't do if this is going to conclude at Singapore."
Washington is strongly backed by Japan and Canada.
While U.S. hopes run high on the technology agreement, U.S. anti-dumping laws are likely to come under heavy criticism during a discussion of competition policy, trade analysts said.
A U.S. law banning imports of tuna caught with nets that kill dolphins is also likely to come under scrutiny during a discussion on trade and environmental policy.
But trade analysts said few issues will be more contentious than a push by the United States to win WTO recognition of basic worker rights.
U.S. officials have said they expect an uphill fight on the labour rights issues, but are hopeful that some progress can be made. Without it, they believe support for global free trade might wane.

"If we are going to expect working people around the world to sustain their support for continued trade liberalisation, with the inevitable dislocations for working people, then working people need to see that there is a positive relationship between trade liberalisation, economic growth and observance of core labour standards," Barshefsky said.

Washington has some European allies, although Britain opposes the idea. But the effort is strongly opposed by Asian countries worried that the rich industrialised nations will use labour rights as a trade protectionist tool.
"It is such a huge club to give protectionists," said Robert O'Quinn, trade specialist with the conservative Heritage Foundation.
But U.S. labour unions consider labour rights an important part of a rules-based global trading system.

The irony, says AFL-CIO international trade specialist Mark Anderson, is that of all the issues the United States is pursuing in the WTO, the only one it is legally obliged to pursue is worker rights.
U.S. laws implementing the global trade agreement that established the WTO, require U.S. trade officials to seek establishment of a WTO panel to examine worker rights, Anderson said.
